newsitem.title: UK: UK Labour to stall EMU sign-up beyond 1999 - analysts.
newsitem.headline: UK Labour to stall EMU sign-up beyond 1999 - analysts.

text.p: Britain's Labour Party is highly unlikely to take the pound into the first wave of a single European currency in 1999 if it wins the next election, leading economists in London's financial centre said on Tuesday.

Quite apart from the vast number of political, structural and economic hurdles to be overcome, recent noises from the top ranks of the party suggest Labour is setting European monetary union (EMU) as a longer-term goal.
"The timetable to really quite tight for them," said Paul Mortimer-Lee, chief economist at Paribas Capital Markets.

Under the Maastricht Treaty, which sets out the timing and conditions for a European single currency due to start in January 1999, countries must in practice decide by the end of this year whether or not they are going to apply.

With the possibility that the British election may not be held until May 22 at the latest, the Labour Party, if it were to become the next government, would have a great deal to get through in little more than seven months.
Labour's foreign affairs spokesman Robin Cook said at the weekend that he viewed the chance that the euro will come into being at all in 1999 at only 50 percent.

Cook, who is widely expected to become foreign secretary if his party wins the election, said that while a Labour government would not rule out entry in 1999, it would examine the state of the single currency in 2002 if it missed out on the start date, and reassess Britain's position.
"If EMU is seen to be successful Labour may at some stage take us in," said John Shepperd, chief UK economist at Yamaichi International in London.
"But the chances of a 1999 entry are extremely unlikely -- as unlikely under Labour as under the Conservatives."

Even if Britain was statistically ready for EMU in 1999, it would be pushing it to pass the necessary legislation through parliament by March 1998, when the decision on who will be "in" and who will be "out" is due to be taken.
Labour has said it will hold a referendum on EMU entry if it decides to go ahead -- an operation which economists say could take four or five months to prepare and complete.
A bid to join the first wave in 1999 would also mean The Bank of England would have to undergo major reform, giving it independence from the government in executing monetary policy.

While Labour is not committed to fully-fledged independence of the central bank -- such as the U.S. Federal Reserve or the German Bundesbank -- it has said it would take steps to make the Bank of England slightly more autonomous than at present.

But Michael Lewis, senior international economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in London, said any hope of Britain being part of EMU in 1999 would have to be accompanied by swift and dramatic action on the central bank by a Labour government.
"It would have to be at the very top of their parliamentary business when they got into government," he said.
"And that would seem such a contentious issue to tackle right at the start of their administration, that we would think they are likely to delay a move until after EMU has actually begun."
The hurdles along the path to a pole position for Britain in 1999 are not just political.
Economically, the convergence taking place between countries such as France, Belgium, Austria, Ireland and Germany is not evident in the UK, economists said.

"UK unemployment has been falling, and continental unemployment has been rising. Our inflation is higher than in Germany or France, and the sterling exchange rate has not been stable," said Mortimer-Lee.
"I just don't see how it could be argued convincingly that the UK economy has converged with the rest of Europe."
-- Kate Kelland, London Newsroom +44 171 542 7708
